runs.text: não ſe manifeſtando em materia de amores, ou

lines.note: This continues Tayexinobi from f0478: enduring without revealing oneself in matters of love. The meaningful consonant in manifeſtando is f, not the draft's long s; the initial não matches the preceding catchword.
The same silent endurance applies to longing, hardships, and illnesses. These are examples governed by the preceding page's verb, not a separate entry.
Tayori is a bearer or opportunity, with an additional sense of help beginning at the line end. The abbreviated Itẽ and the divided A-/juda are preserved.

runs.text: juda, ou couſa que ſerue, preſta, &c. Vt,

lines.note: The additional sense is help or something that serves and is useful. Vt introduces an example showing someone becoming a support to another person.
Fito no tayori ni naru is to be of assistance or become someone else's support. The roman Japanese and italic Portuguese are distinct runs in the scan.
The short continuation supplies the recipient, someone, of that help. It is the final physical row of the example's Portuguese gloss.
Tayori as a verb is explained as approaching or drawing near. The example begins Fito, divided Fi-/tono at the physical line boundary.
Fito no moto ni tayoru means approaching a person. The following added sense starts introduzir-se and continues onto the next row.

runs.text: duzirſe na amizade, ou conuerſação dalguem

lines.note: The added sense is entering another person's friendship or company. The continuation is duzirſe, completing introduzirſe, rather than the OCR dazirſe.

runs.text: pera lhe pedir algũa couſa, ou ſer fauoreci-

lines.note: The purpose of cultivating that relationship is to ask the person for something or receive favor. The printed pera and divided fauoreci- are retained.
The continuation completes being favored by that person. The short row belongs to the same explanation and is not omitted.
Tayorinai and tayori mo nai are first explained as having no bearer or communication. The initial N of Não is plainly present and is restored to the draft.

runs.text: tador, nem recado. ¶ Item, Não ter a-

lines.note: This completes the lack of a bearer or message, then adds the sense of having no shelter or support. The printed a- carries abrigo across the next boundary.

runs.text: brigo nem peßoa de quem ſe valha. ¶

lines.note: A person described this way has nobody to rely on. The following Ta- begins the adverbial expression tayorinǒ vomô, which remains divided across rows.
Tayorinǒ vomô expresses feeling abandoned or without support. The distinct final marks on tayorinǒ and vomô are retained rather than made uniform.
The final equivalent is being without shelter or protection. It closes the preceding example and remains an indented continuation.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de eſtar a couſa

lines.note: Tayotayoto is labeled an adverb describing the manner in which something is soft or weak. The worn word is Modo, not Mado.
The description continues with soft, movable or pliant, and weak. Co- begins the example's cocoro rather than a Portuguese continuation.
Cocoro tayotayoto naru depicts the heart or resolve becoming weak. The Portuguese likewise describes a progressive weakening, with en- carried to the next line.
Fraquecendo completes enfraquecendo. This brief row closes the illustration of wavering or weakening resolve.

runs.text: Meſtre do auto, farſas, ou bailos.

lines.note: Tayǔ is the master of a play, farces, or dances in this entry. The historically specific performance gloss is retained without substituting another modern meaning of the title.

runs.text: Nome de hum caualo que ouue an-

lines.note: Tayǔguro is identified as the name of a horse from long ago. The word an- begins antigamente, continued below.
This continuation supplies antiquity or former times for the named horse. No additional biographical detail is asserted beyond the printed gloss.

Tayumi means becoming slack or weakened. Afroxar has meaningful f, and the internal vowel in debilitarſe is i rather than the draft's u. The r immediately before ſe is extremely faint; its surviving trace, spacing, and the aligned draft support retaining it, with this nonblocking caveat.

Axi ga tayumu means the feet or legs becoming weak. The x has only faint lower traces, but the phrase and the visible remaining letters support Axiga tayumu; the draft's broken A.iga ta umi is not retained. Debilitarenſe keeps the printed n spelling.

runs.text: de maneira que não poßa hum andar. ¶

lines.note: The legs are weakened to the point that one cannot walk. The damaged word is maneira, and Co- starts a new example about the heart or courage.
Cocoro ga tayumu means losing heart or becoming less resolute. The Portuguese says to lose courage or weaken and continues enfra- on the next row.
The first gloss closes with weakening; ito ga tayumu then illustrates a formerly taut thread becoming slack. Afroxar has f and is distinct from an arbitrary long-s spelling choice.

The thread had previously been taut. The aligned draft's estaua is retained: the tall joined stroke in the italic st is not secure evidence for changing short s to long ſ. This row completes the thread example.

Tayutai denotes moving or bobbing upon waves. The headword begins with T, not F; the upright P. marks poetic usage according to the supplied dictionary key and is separate from the italic explanation.
The motion is compared to rocking or balancing. Nami ni tayutǒ illustrates drifting or swaying on waves; the historical spelling and vowel mark are preserved.
Tazai is paraphrased as ta no takara, another's property or treasure. The initial is T and the following Portuguese gives property or riches.
Alheas specifies that the property belongs to someone else. It completes the semantic contrast in ta no takara rather than naming a separate entry.
This Tazzu is simply identified as a tree of that name. The scan supports T rather than OCR F; no unsupported botanical identification is added to the canonical gloss.
The second Tazzu is the poetic word for a crane, equated with tçuru. P. is printed upright, while only the Portuguese Grou is italic.
Tazzugaſa names a particular kind of skin eruption described as sarna. The gloss does not specify a more precise modern diagnosis.
Tazzuna names a horse's reins. The first example repeats the headword, divided before the object marker on the following line.
Tazzuna wo yurusu is to let out or slacken the reins. A second example begins immediately afterward with Taz- continued below.
Tazzuna wo ficayuru means pulling on or holding back the reins. The repeated headword's faint middle strokes remain consistent with the preceding line.
Tazzuna wo caicuru is explained as gathering or wrapping the reins in one's hand. The printed Emburulhar is retained rather than regularized to modern Portuguese.

The hand completes the reins example. A new sense of Tazzuna is equated with Xitavobi, divided Xi-/tavobi across lines. The mark after i has a descending tail in the scan and is corrected from a period to a comma.
Xitavobi identifies an under-sash or lower garment, here glossed Encacho. This is a different sense from the preceding horse-reins entry; the historical Portuguese term is left intact.
Tazzune means to seek or search, with another sense introduced by Item. The initial T is restored from the draft's F.
The added sense is asking or inquiring. This small continuation is semantically significant because the subsequent compounds use both seeking and questioning senses.
Tazzuneai is finding someone by searching. The worn consonant of the past ending is read t, producing ǒta rather than ǒra; the visible cross-stroke and the verb's morphology support that reading.

runs.text: alguem, ou achar a peßoa que ſe buſca.

lines.note: The gloss completes meeting someone or finding the person sought. Its physical inset marks it as a continuation; the draft's flush placement is corrected.
Tazzunecaqe means beginning to ask. The second z is worn, not a comma, and the printed joining aperguntar is preserved; an additional sense continues at the top of column 2.
The added sense of Tazzunecaqe is questioning in an investigative manner. This continues the bottom of column 1 rather than beginning a new headword.
Tazzunedaxi means discovering something through searching. The initial T is visible despite its damaged left stroke; the historical aita past notation is retained.

runs.text: a couſa, ou dar com ella, ou achalla.

lines.note: The explanation gives discovering the thing, coming upon it, or finding it. All three Portuguese equivalents belong to the same compound verb.
Tazzuneidaxi is declared equivalent to the preceding entry. The additional i is genuinely part of this separately printed headword, not a duplicate-row error.
Tazzune motome combines seeking with obtaining or finding. The printed space within the headword is retained, and alcan- is abbreviated with a nasal mark before the line break.
The continuation completes alcançar and adds achar, to obtain or find. It closes the gloss rather than adding a Japanese example.
Tazzuneſaguri means searching and probing or investigating. The headword begins T, not OCR F; the supplied uru and utta endings are not regularized.
The inquiry is undertaken minutely or in detail. Quirir completes inquirir from the preceding row.
Tazzunevabi is searching or inquiring under difficulty. The v represents the Japanese wa element; it is retained as printed, not modernized to w.
Difficulty and labor qualify the preceding searching or inquiry. This supplies the force of the compound's vabi element.

Tazzùra is labeled poetic and equated with ta, a field, with Varzea as the Portuguese equivalent. P. is locally italic before the explanatory form. The draft's grave accent is retained because the small mark is not clear enough to overrule it.
Tazzuſauari means occupying or involving oneself in something. The headword begins T; the scan shows the doubled c in Occuparſe and divides embaraçarſe across the following row.
The verb can mean entangling or involving oneself in some activity. Gacumonni begins an example of engaging in learning or study.

Gacumon ni tazzuſauaru is occupying oneself with study. The repeated verb starts with t, not OCR r. The aligned draft's estudar is retained because the joined italic st does not securely establish long ſ.
Qiǔxen ni tazzuſauaru concerns engagement in arms or warfare. The marked vowel and Japanese spacing remain as printed; the following row supplies the full Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: occupado em guerras, ou acuſtumarſe às armas.

lines.note: The explanation is being occupied in wars or becoming accustomed to arms. The draft's a in occapado is corrected to the visible u, without changing the historical acuſtumarſe spelling.
Tazzuſaye means carrying something with oneself. The headword begins T, and the nasal abbreviation in cõſi- is preserved across the following row.
The example Fiôgu wo tazzuſayuru is carrying arms. This closes the TA section before the separately printed T-before-Ç heading.
Tçu is equated with minato and glossed as a port. This is the first entry after the internal heading; its initial T is ordinary-sized, not an initial spanning multiple physical rows.
The second Tçu means saliva, with Tçubaqi given as an alternative. The example begins tçu ga, with the subject marker joined in the printed form.
Tçu ga kuchi ni tamaru describes saliva collecting in the mouth. The Portuguese mouth-filling-with-water expression is clarified in the next line rather than referring to drinking water.
The clarification specifies saliva or spittle. The abbreviated i, remains inside the printed italic explanatory run.
This Tçuba means lips. The upright X. marks regional Ximo usage according to the supplied dictionary key, rather than forming part of the italic gloss. Its final period shares the label's typeface.

runs.text: Guardas da Catana que he hum circulo

lines.note: The next Tçuba is the guard of a katana, described as a circular fitting. Catana occurs within the Portuguese explanation and is therefore included among optional whole-word typeface terms.

runs.text: de cobre, ou de outro metal redondo que eſtà jũ-

lines.note: The circular guard is made of copper or another metal. The final nasal abbreviation jũ- begins junto and is kept at its physical break.
The fitting sits next to the handles or hilts. This closes the description of the sword guard and retains the printed plural cabos.
Tçubacazzuqi is a metal edging or collar. The next rows specify its location at the scabbard mouth rather than on the blade itself.

runs.text: eſtà na boca da bainha da Catana onde juſta cõ

lines.note: The metal fitting is at the mouth of the katana's scabbard, where it meets the guard. Catana is embedded in Portuguese; the nasal abbreviation cõ is retained.
The continuation names the katana's guard as the adjoining part. The repeated Catana remains an exact typeface-term candidate, not a separate Japanese headword.

runs.text: Tçubacura. l, Tçubacurame. i, Tçu bame.

lines.note: Tçubacura and Tçubacurame are equated with Tçu bame, a swallow. The visibly separated Tçu bame and the divided Portuguese An-/dorinha are preserved.
Dorinha completes the bird name andorinha. The brief continuation belongs to all three synonymous Japanese forms above.

runs.text: Ferro da frecha como boca de

lines.note: Tçubame guchi names an arrowhead shaped like a swallow's mouth. The source's frecha spelling and the space in the Japanese compound are retained.

runs.text: andorinha. ¶ Item. Debrum, ou vinco preto

lines.note: The swallow comparison finishes, followed by a second sense: a black edging or line. The visible paragraph mark before Item is retained as the printed division between these meanings.

runs.text: que fazem ao derredor das bordas das eſcude-

lines.note: That black line is made around the rims of bowls. The Portuguese escudelas is divided after eſcude- at the physical line break.

runs.text: las do arroz charoadas de vermelho.

lines.note: The objects are rice bowls lacquered red. This detail distinguishes the decorative-bowl sense from the earlier arrowhead sense of Tçubame guchi.

runs.text: Lugar da Catana onde eſtão as

lines.note: Tçubamoto denotes the part of the katana where the guard is located. Catana again appears within Portuguese rather than as a standalone headword.
The single-word continuation identifies the guards as the relevant fitting. It closes the definition of Tçubamoto.

runs.text: Hũa erua do campo que da hũa eſ-

lines.note: Tçubana is a field grass producing a white flower spike. The source's general description is kept without importing a more specific botanical classification.

The spike is compared with panha. That unusual-looking comparison word is retained exactly as the aligned draft and scan support it; it is not silently replaced with a guessed modern Portuguese equivalent.

runs.text: Aruore de cujo fructo fazem azei-

lines.note: Tçubaqi is the oil-producing tree, corresponding to the camellia sense rather than the saliva entry below. The damaged b remains part of one continuous headword; the OCR space is removed.
Te completes azeite, oil; the same word also names the tree's flower. The source's joining Aflor is retained.
The saliva sense of Tçubaqi is explicitly preferred to Tçufaqi by the Latin Meliùs quàm, better than. Tçufaqi is an embedded compared term and is marked for optional typeface review.
Tçubaqi wo suru and the alternative Faqu mean to spit. The final Portuguese letter is r, not the draft's t; the alternative remains standalone Japanese rather than an embedded typeface term.
Tçubaſa means the wings of a bird. The printed long s in the Japanese word and the double-s ligature in the Portuguese bird word are retained.
Tçubeta is a kind of shellfish. The initial is T, not OCR A, and the entry ends before the separately placed catchword.
